source.title: New Multiple Descent Phenomena Induced by Heterogeneous Data

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests model-width test-error curves and refines the multiple-descent account: it reports additional interpolation peaks caused by heterogeneous covariance, including in noiseless linear random-feature models.
record.gate_note: The paper reports model-width sweeps on synthetic mixtures and MNIST/CIFAR-10 mixtures, plus theoretical test-error results. Cited findings about model-wise and epoch-wise descent from other work are not rows. Hyperparameter choices and covariance-spectrum estimates used to set up experiments are not outcomes. The reported error magnitudes are generally shown in figures rather than stated numerically; rows record the text-described peak locations and curve behavior.
record.test_reason: The study derives exact test-error curves and runs width sweeps for linear random-feature ridge(less) regression. These bear on V4, since error falls again past m = n. They also bear on V6: it shows triple and multiple peaks, and argues the extra peaks need neither label noise nor nonlinearity. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that covariance heterogeneity across data sources alone yields multiple interpolation peaks (triple or K-fold descent) in linear random-feature models, without label noise or nonlinearity. Peak number and location depend on covariance structure and mixture composition, and group-wise error disparities can be large.
record.recipe_differences: This is a theoretical and empirical study of linear random-feature models trained on heterogeneous covariance mixtures, rather than a reproduction of deep-network double descent. It varies model width and measures source-specific test error.
record.method_sensitivity: Peak locations change with mixture proportion and group sample sizes; covariance-scale separation, spectral structure, and dataset condition affect the observed curves.

fits_no_version.finding: In the proportional-covariance setting E2 = εE1. Near the extra peak, E1 grows as ε^-1/2 while E2 shrinks as ε^1/2, so group-wise error disparity grows at certain widths.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Near interpolation peaks, model scaling can amplify error disparities between data groups with different covariance scale.

fits_no_version.finding: The extra peak's location is set by the sample size of the higher-variance group (m = n1, or cumulative n≤k), not by total n. It moves with mixture proportion while the classical peak stays fixed.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Interpolation thresholds in heterogeneous data occur at cumulative group sample sizes ordered by covariance scale.

record.problems: Empirical error magnitudes are presented in plots rather than as numeric values in the text. Experiments report error bars and run counts, but the text does not state the uncertainty values. The theoretical guarantees assume Gaussian inputs and proportional high-dimensional scaling; broader input distributions are left for future work.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 1 is a cartoon of the theoretical curves, and Figures 3, 4, and 5 repeat conditions captured in the fuller Appendix Figures 6, 9, and 10 or in Theorems 5–7; duplicates were not recorded as separate rows. Appendix Figures 7–8 report covariance spectra rather than test-error outcomes.

untested.parts: No deep networks; only one-layer linear random-feature models with a frozen first layer.
Total n is held fixed while group proportions vary; no sweep of increasing total sample size near the threshold.
Only linear random-feature regression. Other model classes are not tested, and homogeneous data are covered only theoretically (Corollary 4) without a stated curve shape.
No effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across axes.
Whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peaks is not tested; λ is fixed near zero (10^-12 or 10^-6).

missing.what: Group-wise error disparity scaling (E2 = εE1; E1 ~ ε^-1/2, E2 ~ ε^1/2 near the extra peak), with no row.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'challenges' label for V6 is downgraded to limits_scope. The multiple-peak effect is present; only the stated mechanism (noise or variance) is qualified, and regularization dependence is untested. Pointwise error values are figure-only. Theorem 6's proof is omitted.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses one-layer linear random-feature models, not deep networks as specified in this version.
No test-error sweep over training epochs or training time.
The study varies group proportions with total sample size fixed in its mixture experiments; it does not test increasing total training sample size near an interpolation threshold.

Tests linear random-feature models under heterogeneous data, including synthetic, MNIST, and CIFAR-10 mixtures; it does not establish the curve across all model classes or in homogeneous settings generally.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.
Tests multiple peaks with noiseless labels and small regularization, but does not test whether optimally tuned regularization removes peaks.
No re-counting of complexity by an effective number of parameters.

rows.subject: linear random-features model
rows.operation_detail: Analyze source-specific test error for proportional covariance matrices in the ridgeless and small-scale-separation limits.
rows.measure: Group test-error bias versus model width
rows.value: Theorem 5 reports a group-specific singularity at ψ = p1 in addition to the classical one at ψ = 1; for finite sufficiently small ε, the additional singularity is a rounded peak at ψ = p1 + O(ε).
rows.note: Analytical result; the paper identifies the extra peak as arising without label noise or nonlinear activations.

rows.subject: linear random-features model
rows.operation_detail: Analyze the number and locations of interpolation peaks with multiple covariance-scale groups.

conditions.value: Σk = εkΣ, with increasingly separated scales

rows.measure: Group 1 test error versus model size
rows.value: Theorem 6 reports k distinct peaks at m = n≤1, n≤2, …, n≤k; when ϕ > 1 it reports K peaks.
rows.note: The theorem states that each sufficiently separated added group can introduce another interpolation peak.
rows.check: Theorem 6 is analytic and its proof is omitted as 'completely analogous'. Label setting is not stated in the theorem, though the experiments testing it (R7–R10) are noiseless. The row is fine but rests on an unproved extension.

rows.subject: linear random-features model
rows.operation_detail: Analyze test-error curves with proportional covariances and power-law spectrum.
rows.measure: Test error on each group versus parametrization rate ψ
rows.value: Corollary 7 reports two local minima separated by a local maximum at ψ = p1 + O(ε), below the classical threshold ψ = 1; the test-error conclusion also holds with noiseless labels.
rows.note: The paper gives a sufficient condition n1 > H_d,1/H_d,2 for this result.
rows.check: Corollary 7's text says 'suppose ψ > 1', yet it describes a peak at ψ = p1 < 1. This looks like a typo in the source, likely meant ϕ > 1. The condition field should note this inconsistency.

source_check.correct: The sufficient condition is n1 > (H_{d,1})^2/H_{d,2}, not n1 > H_{d,1}/H_{d,2}. Corollary 7 prints ψ > 1 despite describing extrema below ψ = 1; Theorem 5 assumes ϕ > 1, which is the likely intended condition. The proof establishes two minima and an intervening maximum on 0 < ψ < 1, followed by decreasing bias for ψ > 1.

source_check.problem: The row's note drops the square in the sufficient condition and its conditions omit the source's inconsistent ψ > 1 assumption.

relationships.condition: Linear random-feature ridgeless regression on synthetic Gaussian, MNIST and CIFAR-10 heterogeneous mixtures
relationships.reason: Error peaks at m = n and decreases again beyond it. Shown in width sweeps (R1–R34) and analytically, where B ∝ ψη/(ψ−1) decreases for ψ > 1 (R35, R37).
relationships.display_finding: Error peaked at m = n and decreased beyond it in width sweeps, while the analytical term B ∝ ψη/(ψ − 1) decreased for ψ > 1.

source_check.reason: Section 4.1 explicitly reports decreasing error beyond m = n; Theorem 5 and Appendix D.1 establish decreasing bias for ψ > 1. These support renewed improvement beyond interpolation.

relationships.condition: Mixtures with separated covariance scales or spectra
relationships.reason: Curves split into several peaks: an extra peak at m = n1 in two-group mixtures (R1–R6, R11–R34, R35, R37). Four-group mixtures give peaks at 50/150/350/600 (R7–R10), and theory gives K peaks (R36).
relationships.display_finding: Two-group mixtures gained an extra peak at m=n1, four-group mixtures peaked at 50, 150, 350, and 600, and theory predicted K peaks.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Mixtures with separated covariance scales or spectra
source_check.reason: Two-group experiments show an extra peak near m = n1; Figures 3 and 6 report four peaks at 50, 150, 350 and 600. This supports V6's multiple-peak component; optimal regularization is untested.

relationships.condition: Noiseless labels, linear activations, heterogeneous input covariance
relationships.reason: With σ = 0 the variance term vanishes, yet both the extra and the classical peaks arise in the bias term (R35, R37) and in noiseless experiments (R1–R34). So 'driven by label noise or variance' needs qualifying: input-covariance heterogeneity alone suffices.
relationships.display_finding: At σ = 0, the variance term vanishes, yet both classical and additional peaks arise in bias and appear experimentally.

source_check.condition: Noiseless labels, linear activations, heterogeneous input covariance
source_check.reason: The study's variance term vanishes with label noise, while its bias retains classical and additional peaks. This qualifies the proposed attribution without showing descent itself absent or reversed.

source_check.notes: The authors-conclusion paraphrase is accurate; bias here includes randomness from the design and frozen features, so its averaging convention matters. Figures 3 and 6 explicitly state peak locations but do not separately state the post-600 decline; optimal removal of peaks by regularization is untested.

statements.correction: Section 2.1 assumes positive-definite covariances. Section 4.1 reports additional peaks with power-law spectra and with positive isotropic covariance scales. For n = 1000, changing p1 from 1/4 to 1/2 to 3/4 moves the extra peak from m = 250 to 500 to 750; the classical peak remains at m = 1000.
statements.problem: The mixture-proportion claim is supported. The full-rank/near-degenerate restriction is not established by this study and is overbroad if applied to its heterogeneous covariances.

reader_labels.label: supports
